question: What is the primary advantage of the intravenous route over oral administration?

options.A: Absence of local site pain
options.B: Simpler technique for nurses
options.C: Faster onset of drug action
options.D: Lower risk of fluid overload

explanation: Injecting fluids directly into the bloodstream skips the digestive system, allowing medications to work almost immediately. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why does intravenous therapy carry a higher risk of severe adverse reactions compared to oral medications?

options.A: Patients are usually sicker when they receive IV drugs
options.B: Veins absorb medications much faster than stomach walls
options.C: Intravenous medications are always chemically stronger
options.D: The administered substance cannot be retrieved once injected

explanation: Direct entry into the circulation means an incorrect dose or allergic reaction takes effect immediately with no way to pump the stomach. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which clinical situation requires the use of intravenous fluid therapy?

options.A: Routine daily multivitamin supplementation at home
options.B: Chronic stable hypertension controlled by diet
options.C: Severe dehydration requiring rapid fluid replacement
options.D: Mild headache treatable with swallowing pills

explanation: When fluids must be restored quickly or the gut cannot absorb them, the intravenous route is the fastest solution. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h2)

question: A patient needs an IV line inserted. Which limb area MUST be avoided?

options.A: A forearm showing faint bruising from a previous blood test
options.B: The cephalic vein area of an adult male patient
options.C: The dorsal surface of the non-dominant hand
options.D: An arm with a surgically created dialysis fistula

explanation: Dialysis access points must be protected from punctures, blood draws, and IV lines to preserve blood flow for kidney failure treatment. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of priming extension tubing with normal saline before starting an IV?

options.A: To remove trapped air and prevent air embolisms
options.B: To warm the tubing up to body temperature
options.C: To test if the syringe plunger moves smoothly
options.D: To dilute any medication given later on

explanation: Clearing all air bubbles from the line stops air from entering the patient's bloodstream during cannulation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why should a nurse inspect product packaging expiration dates before gathering IV supplies?

options.A: Hospital management penalizes nurses who waste old stock
options.B: Plastic catheters become too hard to puncture skin over time
options.C: Expired items may have lost their sterile barrier
options.D: Saline flushes expire and turn acidic inside plastic

explanation: Sterile packaging guarantees infection prevention; if the date has passed, sterility is no longer assured. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h3)

question: Where should a nurse begin looking for a suitable vein for initial cannulation?

options.A: Most distal areas of the upper extremities
options.B: Delicate veins directly over wrist joint creases
options.C: Large veins located in the lower extremities
options.D: Proximal veins close to the upper shoulder

explanation: Starting low on the hand or forearm preserves higher vein sites for future access if the current line fails. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h4)

question: What physical characteristic indicates that a vein is a poor choice for cannulation?

options.A: The vein bounces back softly when pressed
options.B: The vein is clearly visible under light skin
options.C: The vein feels hard, rigid, and cord-like
options.D: The vein disappears temporarily when warmed

explanation: Hard or sclerosed veins are damaged and fragile, meaning they will easily rupture or fail to hold a cannula. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h4)

question: What visual sign inside the catheter hub confirms that the needle has successfully entered the vein?

options.A: A sudden drop in local skin temperature
options.B: Clear fluid filling the plastic chamber
options.C: Air bubbles moving up the tubing
options.D: A flashback of dark red blood

explanation: Blood entering the back of the needle hub proves the tip is sitting inside the blood vessel lumen. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why must an antiseptic skin prep air-dry completely before inserting an IV catheter?

options.A: To allow the chemical time to kill microorganisms effectively
options.B: To ensure the vein stays dilated and easy to see
options.C: To prevent the sticky dressing from sliding off wet skin
options.D: To keep the patient from feeling a burning sensation

explanation: Antiseptics like chlorhexidine require contact time and drying to achieve their full germ-killing effect. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h5)

question: What action must a nurse take before giving a direct IV medication through an existing line?

options.A: Increase the main infusion fluid flow to maximum speed
options.B: Disconnect the entire cannula and replace the dressing
options.C: Warm the medication bottle in a basin of hot water
options.D: Flush the line with normal saline to check patency

explanation: Flushing ensures the catheter is open, working properly, and clear of incompatible drugs before the new medication enters. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is checking drug compatibility important when administering multiple intravenous infusions?

options.A: Incompatible drugs can react and form solid crystals that block the catheter
options.B: Combining medications changes the colour of the plastic infusion tubing
options.C: Mixing drugs always causes the patient to develop a skin rash
options.D: Incompatible solutions neutralize each other and make nurses look careless

explanation: Chemical reactions between mixed drugs can create precipitates that clog the line and endanger the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h6)

question: How often should a nurse routinely inspect a standard peripheral intravenous site?

options.A: At least once every nursing shift
options.B: Once every three days when fluids finish
options.C: Every time the patient eats a meal
options.D: Only when the infusion pump starts beeping

explanation: Regular checks catch early signs of complications like swelling, redness, or leaking before they turn severe. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h7)

question: Which finding during a routine IV assessment suggests the dressing needs immediate replacement?

options.A: The intravenous fluid bag is half full of normal saline
options.B: The patient reports sleeping well through the entire night
options.C: The dressing edges are lifting and exposing the insertion site
options.D: The extension tubing is coiled neatly on the bed sheet

explanation: Lifting dressings lose their sterile seal, increasing the risk of bacteria entering the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary symptom that distinguishes extravasation from simple fluid infiltration?

options.A: Severe blistering, tissue damage, or necrosis
options.B: A slight slowing of the gravity drip rate
options.C: Sudden cooling of the surrounding skin area
options.D: Leaking of clear fluid around the adhesive tape

explanation: Extravasation happens with vesicant drugs that destroy local tissue, whereas simple infiltration involves non-harmful fluids. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h8)

question: Which physical sign strongly indicates that a patient is developing phlebitis at their IV site?

options.A: Clear fluid leaks out from beneath the transparent dressing
options.B: The surrounding skin feels very cold and appears swollen
options.C: A red, warm, tender streak following the path of the vein
options.D: The infusion pump stops working and sounds an occlusion alarm

explanation: Phlebitis is vein inflammation, showing up as redness, warmth, and pain along the vessel path. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h8)

question: What essential check must a nurse perform immediately after removing an IV catheter?

options.A: Rinse the puncture site with cold tap water
options.B: Measure the exact volume of blood left in the hub
options.C: Soak the removed plastic tubing in an antiseptic jar
options.D: Inspect the catheter tip to ensure it is fully intact

explanation: Checking the tip confirms that no broken plastic piece remains inside the patient's vein. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h9)

question: A nurse is removing an IV line from a patient taking daily blood-thinning medication. What action is most important?

options.A: Skip the sterile gauze pad and apply transparent tape right away
options.B: Remove the cannula at a steep 45-degree angle to seal the skin
options.C: Apply firm, prolonged pressure to the site until bleeding stops completely
options.D: Massage the puncture site vigorously to stimulate local circulation

explanation: Patients on blood thinners bleed longer, so extended direct pressure prevents large hematomas from forming. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h9)

question: Which detail is NOT required when documenting a new peripheral IV insertion?

options.A: The catheter gauge and anatomical location
options.B: The brand name of the soap used for handwashing
options.C: The patient's response and tolerance to the procedure
options.D: The date and exact time of the insertion

explanation: Standard hand hygiene is assumed; charting focuses on the specific procedure details like size, location, time, and patient response. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h10)

question: Why is accurate and prompt charting of IV care crucial for nursing practice?

options.A: It is the only way hospital administrators calculate nurse salaries
options.B: It stops patients from asking nurses repetitive questions about fluids
options.C: It provides a clear legal record of care and ensures safe continuity among staff
options.D: It replaces the need for verbal shift handovers between nursing teams

explanation: Good documentation proves professional standards were met and helps the next shift monitor the site safely. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h10)
